analysis.title: The sell-off has likely gone too far (CIO View: Crude oil)
key_insights: Brent is down around USD 20/bbl since the end of October. The main driver was a strong recovery in Middle Eastern crude exports, and the risk-off move in equity markets added pressure.

Petro-Logistics estimates Gulf crude and condensate exports (including Oman and pipeline flows bypassing the Strait) at about 19.5 mbpd in October, against a pre-war level of 19.9 mbpd in February. Refined-product exports stayed well below pre-war levels. US naval escorts facilitated the crude recovery.
UBS says the market has become too comfortable with the supply outlook. The October rebound in Gulf exports is not a normalization of the oil market.

Attacks on ships have intensified, with 19 reported and confirmed incidents in the first 18 days of November. Middle Eastern crude exports have fallen to an estimated 15.7 mbpd in the first half of November.
US military support is costly, and it is unclear how long the US will sustain this level of involvement.
China is stepping up crude imports. Imports recovered to nearly 10 mbpd in October and could rise well above 11 mbpd in November, which would absorb part of the October build in barrels on water.

The global inventory buffer remains depleted. The IEA estimates observed inventories have fallen by 462 million barrels since the start of the war, and on-land stocks are at their lowest since at least 2016.
Positioning is cleaner after the sell-off. Money managers have cut Brent net longs to the lowest level in more than four months, and WTI net longs are at the lowest since January.
UBS sees an attractive near-term risk-reward in crude oil and expects prices to recover. Its main risk is a durable political agreement that normalizes Middle Eastern production.
UBS Brent forecasts (end of period): 95.0 in Mar 27, 90.0 in Jun 27, 85.0 in Sep 27, 80.0 in Dec 27. Spot Brent was 91.9 on 20 Nov 26.

sector_views.rationale: UBS expects crude prices to recover from here, citing depleted inventories, fading emergency stock releases, reduced speculative positioning, rising Chinese imports and renewed disruption to Gulf flows.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Brent is down about USD 20/bbl since the end of October. UBS sees the sell-off as overdone.
UBS expects a near-term recovery toward 95 by March 2027, then a gradual decline.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The buffer against further supply disruption is depleted, with on-land stocks at their lowest since at least 2016.

trade_ideas.description: Long crude oil (Brent/WTI) for a near-term price recovery
trade_ideas.rationale: Visible inventories remain well below pre-war levels, the bulk of emergency stock releases is behind us, and speculative positioning has been substantially reduced.
trade_ideas.risk: A durable political agreement that normalizes Middle Eastern production.

risk_factors: A durable political agreement that normalizes Middle Eastern production.
US reluctance or inability to sustain naval support for Gulf exports.
The risk-off environment in equity markets could keep pressuring oil prices.
charts_described: Brent crude oil chart shows spot of 91.9 on 20 Nov 26 and UBS end-of-period forecasts of 95.0 (Mar 27), 90.0 (Jun 27), 85.0 (Sep 27) and 80.0 (Dec 27).

Money manager positioning chart in Brent and WTI futures and options, in million barrels: the text says Brent net longs are at the lowest in more than four months and WTI net longs at the lowest since January.
vol_and_positioning: Money managers have cut Brent net-long positions to their lowest level in more than four months.
WTI net longs are at their lowest since January.
UBS says speculative positioning has been substantially reduced, leaving prices sensitive to downside surprises in supply.
geopolitical: Attacks on tankers and infrastructure in the Middle East have intensified, with 19 reported and confirmed incidents in the first 18 days of November.
US naval escorts supported the recovery of Gulf crude exports, and UBS questions how long the US will sustain this involvement.
A durable political agreement that normalizes Middle Eastern production is the key risk to UBS's bullish oil view.

tension_points.bull_case: UBS argues prices should recover: Middle Eastern exports fell to about 15.7 mbpd in early November, Chinese imports are rising, inventories are depleted and speculative positioning is cleaned out.
tension_points.bear_case: The October recovery in Gulf exports to 19.5 mbpd, near the pre-war 19.9 mbpd, drove the sell-off, and a durable political agreement could normalize Middle Eastern production.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A durable political agreement that normalizes Middle Eastern production.

theme_stances.key_argument: Visible inventories remain well below pre-war levels, emergency stock releases are mostly behind us, and speculative positioning has been substantially reduced.
theme_stances.evidence: This supports our view that oil prices should recover from here.
